newsitem.title: PUERTO RICO: Hurricane Hortense edges toward Puerto Rico.
newsitem.headline: Hurricane Hortense edges toward Puerto Rico.

text.p: Schools and government offices were closed in the U.S. Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico on Monday as Hurricane Hortense slowly carried its 80 mph (130 kph) winds and heavy rains through the northeastern Caribbean.

At 5 p.m. EDT (2100 GMT), Hortense's centre was 95 miles (150 km) southeast of Ponce, Puerto Rico's second city, near latitude 16.8 north longitude 66.0 west, and moving northwest at seven mph (11 kph), the National Hurricane Centre said.

A hurricane warning was in effect for Puerto Rico and a tropical storm warning for the U.S. and British Virgin Islands. The Dominican Republic -- next in Hortense's path -- posted a hurricane watch for parts of its south coast.

Tropical storm force winds were lashing the Virgin Islands Monday, and mariners were urged to stay in port as seas rose. Shelters were opened and power flashed on and off in Charlotte Amalie, the territory's capital. Several cruise ships were rerouted to avoid Hortense, leaving the island's cruise docks empty. Airports on the three islands were closed.
But residents said they had experienced worse in July when Hurricane Bertha brushed the islands.
"We've been experiencing gusty winds but no rain yet," said Herb Shoenbaum, who works at a radio station on Saint Croix. "So far, it's a lot less than Bertha."

In Puerto Rico, supermarkets were busy on Monday as residents stocked up. The first strong winds hit the islands of Culebra and Vieques, off the island's eastern end, and local forecasters said the U.S. territory's mainland should expect strong winds soon, with hurricane-force gusts possible for the island beginning before dawn on Tuesday.

The Puerto Rico Civil Defence prepared to open 300 shelters, police leave was cancelled and the entire force was put on 24-hour alert. Gov. Pedro Rossello banned the sale of alcohol, ordered public schools closed and gave most government workers the day off.
Watches are posted when hurricane or tropical storm conditions are expected within 36 hours. A warning indicates the arrival of such conditions within 24 hours.

Hortense's maximum sustained winds had risen to near 80 mph (130 kph) by midday, making the storm a relatively low Category 1 hurricane. "It had started dying out yesterday morning, and then all of a sudden it started back up again," said National Hurricane Centre meteorologist Trisha Wallace.

Forecasters said Hortense was likely to strengthen Tuesday, saying the system was heading for landfall in the Dominican Republic. They warned that heavy rains of 12 inches (30 cm) or more could trigger deadly mudslides and flash floods. Some 2,000 people were killed by mudslides and flooding in Haiti, west of the Dominican Republic on Hispaniola island, when Tropical Storm Gordon struck in 1994.

Forecasters also said Hortense could bring storm surge flooding to Puerto Rico's southern coast. Hurricane-force winds extended up to 60 miles (95 km) from Hortense's centre and tropical storm force winds spread 175 miles (280 km).
It was too early for forecasters to predict whether Hortense might hit the mainland United States as it moved slowly west, hundreds of miles (kilometres) from Florida.
